chapters.title: Income from Other Sources
chapters.summary: Residual head: dividends, interest, winnings, gifts and property received for inadequate consideration, family pension and permitted deductions.
chapters.lawAsOf: Income-tax Act 2025 as amended by Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: Residual head and specific incomes
lesson.body:
Income from other sources is charged under section 92 of the 2025 Act (sections 56 to 59 of the 1961 Act). It is a **residual** head: income not taxable under any other head falls here. Some incomes are always taxed here:

- **Dividends** (taxable in the hands of shareholders).
- **Winnings** from lotteries, crossword puzzles, races including horse races, card games, gambling or betting: taxed at a flat **30%** (old section 115BB). No expense, no deduction and no basic exemption is allowed against them. Net winnings from online games have their own 30% charge (old section 115BBJ).
- **Interest on securities**, bank deposits and other interest (if not business income).
- **Gifts and property received** without or for inadequate consideration (old section 56(2)(x)).
- **Family pension** received by legal heirs of a deceased employee.
- Income from letting of machinery, plant or furniture, and composite letting with a building where the lettings are inseparable, if not business income.
- Interest on compensation or enhanced compensation (50% deduction allowed).

lesson.heading: Gifts: sum of money and property
lesson.body:
| Receipt by any person | Taxable amount |
| --- | --- |
| Sum of money without consideration | Whole amount, if aggregate in the year exceeds ₹50,000 |
| Immovable property without consideration | Stamp duty value, if it exceeds ₹50,000 |
| Immovable property for inadequate consideration | SDV minus consideration, if the difference exceeds the higher of ₹50,000 and 10% of consideration |
| Other property (shares, jewellery, paintings, bullion) without consideration | Aggregate FMV, if it exceeds ₹50,000 |
| Other property for inadequate consideration | FMV minus consideration, if the difference exceeds ₹50,000 |

**Not taxable** when received:

- from a **relative** (spouse, brother or sister, brother or sister of the spouse, brother or sister of either parent, any lineal ascendant or descendant, and lineal ascendant or descendant of the spouse, and spouses of these persons);
- on the occasion of the individual's **marriage**;
- under a will or by inheritance, or in contemplation of death;
- from a local authority, a registered charitable trust or institution, or an educational / medical institution;
- from an HUF by its member.

The ₹50,000 limit is an aggregate threshold: if gifts from non-relatives total ₹55,000, all ₹55,000 is taxable.

lesson.heading: Deductions and family pension
lesson.body:
Deductions (section 93 of the 2025 Act; old section 57):

- Family pension: **lower of one-third of family pension and ₹25,000** under the new regime; ₹15,000 under the old regime.
- Any other expenditure laid out wholly and exclusively for earning the income (not capital, not personal).
- Interest on compensation: 50% of such interest.

Not deductible: personal expenses, interest payable outside India without TDS, wealth-tax, and any expense against winnings.

The Finance Act, 2026 withdrew the deduction for interest expenditure against dividend and mutual fund income; do not allow it for tax year 2026-27.

Format:

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Dividend | xxx |
| Interest on deposits and securities | xxx |
| Family pension less deduction | xxx |
| Gifts taxable | xxx |
| Winnings (taxed separately at 30%) | xxx |
| **Income from other sources** | **xxx** |

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Taxing only the excess over ₹50,000 for gifts. Once the aggregate crosses ₹50,000, the whole is taxable.
- Treating a gift from a cousin or friend as from a relative. Cousins are not relatives under this definition.
- Allowing basic exemption or Chapter VI-A deductions against lottery winnings.
- Taxing the net amount received from a lottery. Gross up for TDS: the gross winning is taxable.
- Using 10% of SDV instead of 10% of consideration for the tolerance on immovable property.

keyPoints: Residual head (section 92 of the 2025 Act; old section 56).
Winnings: flat 30% on gross amount, no deductions, no basic exemption.
Gifts of money above ₹50,000 aggregate: whole amount taxable; relatives, marriage, will and inheritance excluded.
Immovable property for inadequate consideration: taxable if SDV - consideration > higher of ₹50,000 and 10% of consideration.
Family pension deduction: lower of 1/3 and ₹25,000 (new) / ₹15,000 (old).
Interest on enhanced compensation: 50% deduction.

questions.explanation: SDV - consideration = 50,00,000 - 40,00,000 = 10,00,000. This exceeds the higher of ₹50,000 and 10% of consideration (₹4,00,000), so ₹10,00,000 is taxable.

questions.prompt: What amount of lottery income is included in Mr. Ajay's income, and at what rate is it taxed?
questions.explanation: The gross amount is 70,000 / 70% = ₹1,00,000. Winnings are taxed at a flat 30% with no deduction.

questions.prompt: If the land's stamp duty value were ₹43,50,000, nothing would be taxable in Mr. Ajay's hands on the purchase.
questions.explanation: The difference would be ₹3,50,000, which does not exceed 10% of consideration (₹4,00,000).

questions.prompt: Mrs. Lalitha receives family pension of ₹3,00,000 in tax year 2026-27 and stays in the new regime. Compute the taxable family pension.
Mr. Hari, a resident, wins ₹2,00,000 in a TV quiz show. His other income is ₹3,00,000 (new regime). Compute tax payable on the winnings including cess.
questions.explanation: Winnings are taxed at a flat 30%: 2,00,000 x 30% = 60,000; cess 4% = 2,400; total ₹62,400. Unused basic exemption cannot be set against winnings, and the rebate is not available against special-rate income under the new regime.

questions.prompt: Mr. R receives a painting worth ₹80,000 as a gift from his friend. The amount taxable is:
options: Nil, as a painting is not a sum of money
Nil, as paintings are personal effects
questions.explanation: A painting is 'property' for this provision. FMV above ₹50,000 received without consideration is fully taxable.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a 'relative' for exemption of gifts received by an individual?
questions.explanation: Brother or sister of the spouse is a relative. Cousins and nephews are not in the list.

questions.prompt: Interest received on enhanced compensation of ₹4,00,000 is taxable under other sources at:
questions.explanation: A deduction of 50% of such interest is allowed, so ₹2,00,000 is taxable in the year of receipt.

questions.prompt: Which receipts by an individual are NOT taxable under the gift provisions? Select all that apply.
options: ₹2,00,000 received under the will of an uncle
Gifts of ₹3,00,000 received on his marriage
questions.explanation: Gifts from a lineal ascendant, under a will, and on the occasion of marriage are excluded. Friends and cousins are not relatives.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: winnings from lotteries and races are taxed at a flat rate of ___% (before surcharge and cess).
questions.explanation: Old section 115BB charges 30%, without any deduction or basic exemption.

questions.prompt: Explain the taxability of property received without or for inadequate consideration under the 1961 Act, section 56(2)(x).
questions.answer:
- Applies to any person (individual, HUF, firm, company).
- Money: aggregate receipts without consideration above ₹50,000 in a year are fully taxable.
- Immovable property without consideration: stamp duty value taxable if above ₹50,000; for inadequate consideration, SDV minus consideration is taxable if it exceeds the higher of ₹50,000 and 10% of consideration.
- Movable property (shares, jewellery, bullion, drawings, paintings, sculptures, archaeological collections): aggregate FMV above ₹50,000 if no consideration; FMV minus consideration if the difference exceeds ₹50,000.
- Exclusions: receipts from relatives, on marriage, under will or inheritance, from local authorities and registered trusts, and specified business reorganisations.
- Cost of such property for later capital gains is the value already taxed.
- The 2025 Act retains these rules under the other-sources head.

chapters.title: Clubbing, Set-off and Carry Forward of Losses, Deductions
chapters.summary: Income of other persons included in an assessee's income, inter-source and inter-head set-off, carry forward of losses, and Chapter VI-A deductions under both regimes.
chapters.lawAsOf: Income-tax Act 2025 as amended by Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: Clubbing of income
lesson.body:
Clubbing provisions (section 99 of the 2025 Act; sections 60 to 65 of the 1961 Act) tax one person on income legally belonging to another.

| Situation (1961 Act) | Clubbed in the hands of |
| --- | --- |
| Transfer of income without transfer of asset (60) | Transferor |
| Revocable transfer of assets (61) | Transferor |
| Remuneration of spouse from a concern in which the individual has substantial interest (20% or more voting power or profit share), unless the spouse has technical or professional qualification and the income is attributable to it (64(1)(ii)) | The spouse with substantial interest (if both, the one with higher total income before clubbing) |
| Income from assets transferred to spouse without adequate consideration, other than under an agreement to live apart (64(1)(iv)) | Transferor |
| Income from assets transferred to son's wife without adequate consideration (64(1)(vi)) | Transferor |
| Income of a minor child (64(1A)) | Parent whose total income (before clubbing) is greater; if parents' marriage does not subsist, the parent maintaining the child |

Minor's income is **not** clubbed if it arises from manual work or from activity involving the minor's skill, talent or specialised knowledge, or if the minor has a disability of the kind specified for the disability deduction. In the old regime, exemption of up to **₹1,500 per minor child** is allowed on clubbed income (old section 10(32)).

Income on accretion (interest earned on clubbed income that is reinvested) is not clubbed; it is the transferee's own income.

lesson.heading: Set-off and carry forward of losses
lesson.body:
Order: first **intra-head** set-off (one source against another under the same head), then **inter-head** set-off, then brought forward losses.

| Loss | Current-year set-off | Carry forward |
| --- | --- | --- |
| House property | Any head, up to ₹2,00,000 a year (old regime); not against other heads in the new regime | 8 years, against house property income only |
| Business (non-speculative) | Any head except salary | 8 years, against business income |
| Speculation business | Only speculation profit | 4 years |
| Specified business (old 35AD) | Only specified business profit | Indefinitely |
| Short-term capital loss | STCG or LTCG | 8 years, against STCG or LTCG |
| Long-term capital loss | Only LTCG | 8 years, only LTCG |
| Owning and maintaining race horses | Only that activity | 4 years |
| Unabsorbed depreciation | Any head except salary | Indefinitely |

No loss can be set off against winnings from lotteries, races and the like. Losses other than house property loss and unabsorbed depreciation can be carried forward only if the return of the loss year was filed **by the due date**.

The set-off provisions sit in sections 108 to 121 of the 2025 Act.

lesson.heading: Deductions from gross total income (old regime)
lesson.body:
Total deductions cannot exceed GTI, and are not allowed against special-rate capital gains or winnings. Under the new default regime only a few are available, chiefly employer NPS contribution (old 80CCD(2)), Agnipath contribution (80CCH) and new employment (80JJAA).

| Deduction (1961 Act) | Main limit |
| --- | --- |
| 80C (section 123 of the 2025 Act): LIC premium, PPF, EPF, ELSS, tuition fees for 2 children, housing loan principal, 5-year bank FD, NSC, Sukanya Samriddhi | ₹1,50,000 (with 80CCC and 80CCD(1)) |
| 80CCD(1B): own NPS contribution | Additional ₹50,000 |
| 80D: health insurance | Self / family ₹25,000 (₹50,000 if senior); parents ₹25,000 (₹50,000 if senior); preventive health check-up ₹5,000 within these; no cash premium |
| 80E: interest on education loan | Actual interest, 8 years |
| 80G: donations | 100% or 50%, with or without qualifying limit of 10% of adjusted GTI; cash above ₹2,000 not allowed |
| 80GG: rent paid without HRA | Least of rent - 10% of total income, ₹5,000 per month, 25% of total income |
| 80TTA: savings interest (non-senior) | ₹10,000 |
| 80TTB: interest of resident senior citizen | ₹50,000 |
| 80U / 80DD: disability | ₹75,000 (₹1,25,000 severe) |

Worked example (80C and 80D): LIC 60,000 + PPF 1,00,000 + tuition fees 40,000 + housing loan principal 30,000 = 2,30,000, restricted to 1,50,000. Mediclaim for self ₹30,000 (allowed 25,000) and senior parents ₹55,000 (allowed 50,000). Total deduction ₹2,25,000.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Setting off business loss against salary.
- Setting off LTCL against STCG.
- Clubbing a minor's income from skill (such as a music competition prize).
- Clubbing the minor's income with the father by default; it goes to the parent with higher income.
- Allowing 80C-type deductions under the new regime.
- Allowing 80D for a premium paid in cash, or 80G for a cash donation above ₹2,000.
- Forgetting that carry forward needs a return filed by the due date (except house property loss and unabsorbed depreciation).

keyPoints: Minor's income clubbed with the parent having higher income; ₹1,500 exemption per child (old regime); skill income and disabled minor's income not clubbed.
Assets gifted to spouse or son's wife: income clubbed with transferor; accretion not clubbed.
HP loss: ₹2 lakh inter-head (old regime), none in new regime; carry forward 8 years.
Business loss not against salary; speculation loss only against speculation profit (4 years).
LTCL only against LTCG; STCL against both; 8 years.
New regime: only employer NPS (80CCD(2)), 80CCH and 80JJAA type deductions.

cases.title: Case: The Sharma family
cases.body:
Mr. Arvind Sharma and Mrs. Neelam Sharma, both residents, opt for the old regime for tax year 2026-27.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Mr. Sharma's income from salary | 15,00,000 |
| Mrs. Sharma's income from salary | 6,00,000 |
| Interest on FD made by Mrs. Sharma from ₹10,00,000 gifted to her by Mr. Sharma in 2025 | 80,000 |

questions.explanation: Income of a minor from activity involving skill or talent is not clubbed; it is assessed as the minor's own income (through her guardian).

questions.explanation: Only income from the transferred asset is clubbed. Income from reinvestment of that income (accretion) is the spouse's own income.

questions.prompt: If Mrs. Sharma's income before clubbing were higher than Mr. Sharma's, Kunal's FD interest would be clubbed with:
questions.explanation: A minor's income is clubbed with the parent whose total income (before clubbing) is greater.

questions.explanation: Qualifying amount = lower of donation (1,00,000) and 10% of adjusted GTI (80,000) = 80,000. Deduction = 50% of 80,000 = ₹40,000.

questions.prompt: Explain the clubbing of a minor child's income.
questions.answer:
- Old section 64(1A); retained in section 99 of the 2025 Act.
- All income of a minor child is clubbed with the income of the parent whose total income (before clubbing) is greater; if the marriage does not subsist, with the parent who maintains the minor.
- Once clubbed with one parent, it stays with that parent in later years unless the Assessing Officer is satisfied a change is needed.
- Not clubbed: income from manual work or from activity involving the minor's skill, talent or specialised knowledge and experience; income of a minor with a specified disability.
- In the old regime the parent gets an exemption up to ₹1,500 per minor child (old section 10(32)).
- A minor child includes a step child and an adopted child.

chapters.title: Total Income, Tax Liability, Advance Tax, TDS/TCS and Returns
chapters.summary: Bringing the heads together into total income and tax payable, then paying it through advance tax, TDS and TCS, interest for defaults, and filing the return.
chapters.lawAsOf: Income-tax Act 2025 as amended by Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: Computation of total income and tax liability
lesson.body:
Format for an individual (tax year 2026-27):

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Income from salaries | xxx |
| Income from house property | xxx |
| Profits and gains of business or profession | xxx |
| Capital gains (STCG 111A, other STCG, LTCG 112A, other LTCG shown separately) | xxx |
| Income from other sources | xxx |
| Add: Clubbed income; less: set-off of losses | xxx |
| **Gross total income** | **xxx** |
| Less: Deductions (only those allowed in the chosen regime) | (xxx) |
| **Total income (rounded to nearest ₹10)** | **xxx** |
| Tax on special-rate income (111A 20%, 112A 12.5%, 112 12.5%, winnings 30%) | xxx |
| Tax on balance at slab rates | xxx |
| Less: Rebate (resident individual) | (xxx) |
| Add: Surcharge, then cess @ 4% | xxx |
| Less: Relief (arrears of salary, double taxation) | (xxx) |
| Less: TDS, TCS and advance tax | (xxx) |
| **Tax payable / refundable (rounded to nearest ₹10)** | **xxx** |

A resident individual may use unused basic exemption against 111A, 112 and 112A gains, but not against winnings. Chapter VI-A deductions are not allowed against special-rate gains.

lesson.heading: Advance tax and interest
lesson.body:
Advance tax is payable if tax liability for the year (after TDS / TCS) is **₹10,000 or more** (old sections 207 to 211). A resident senior citizen without business or profession income is exempt.

| Due date | Cumulative instalment (general) | Presumptive cases (44AD / 44ADA) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 15 June | 15% | - |
| 15 September | 45% | - |
| 15 December | 75% | - |
| 15 March | 100% | 100% |

Interest (simple, per month or part of a month):

| Section (1961 Act) | Default | Rate and period |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 234A | Return filed after the due date | 1% per month on tax unpaid, from the day after the due date to the date of filing |
| 234B | Advance tax paid is less than 90% of assessed tax | 1% per month on the shortfall, from 1 April after the tax year to the date of determination (self-assessment) |
| 234C | Instalments short of 12%, 36%, 75%, 100% at the four dates | 1% per month for 3 months (1 month for the last instalment) on the shortfall against 15%, 45%, 75%, 100% |

Worked example (234B): assessed tax (net of TDS) ₹1,60,000; advance tax paid ₹1,00,000, which is below 90% (₹1,44,000). Shortfall ₹60,000. Tax paid with the return on 31 July 2027: April to July = 4 months. Interest = 60,000 x 1% x 4 = **₹2,400**.

lesson.heading: TDS and TCS
lesson.body:
The 2025 Act consolidates TDS into **section 392** (salary) and **section 393** (all other payments, set out in tables), and TCS into **section 394**. Exam questions often still use the 1961 section names below.

| Payment (1961 Act) | Rate |
| --- | --- |
| Salary (192) | Average rate on estimated income of the year, under the regime chosen by the employee |
| Interest other than on securities (194A) | 10% |
| Payment to contractors (194C) | 1% to individual / HUF, 2% to others |
| Commission or brokerage (194H) | 2% |
| Rent (194-I) | 2% plant and machinery; 10% land, building, furniture |
| Fees for professional services (194J) | 10% (2% for technical services, royalty for films, call centres) |
| Lottery and crossword winnings (194B) | 30% |
| Payee without PAN (206AA) | Higher of 20% and the normal rate (generally) |

Thresholds were revised by the Finance Act, 2025 and the 2025 Act; check the current table before applying them.

The deductor deposits TDS with the government, files quarterly statements and issues certificates (Form 16 for salary, Form 16A for others under the 1961 Act; the 2025 Act renumbers the forms). The deductee claims credit as shown in the annual information statement.

**TCS** is collected by the seller on specified sales and remittances (scrap, alcoholic liquor, forest produce, motor vehicles above ₹10 lakh, overseas tour packages and LRS remittances). The Finance Act, 2026 rationalised several TCS rates; use the ICAI-applicable table.

lesson.heading: Return of income
lesson.body:
Return filing is governed by section 263 of the 2025 Act (corresponds to section 139 of the 1961 Act).

- A company and a firm must file every year, whatever the income.
- An individual must file if total income (before certain exemptions and deductions) exceeds the basic exemption limit, and also in specified cases such as deposit above ₹1 crore in current accounts, foreign travel expenditure above ₹2 lakh or electricity bills above ₹1 lakh in the year, or holding foreign assets as a resident.
- **Due dates**: 31 October for assessees whose accounts are audited; 30 November for transfer pricing cases; 31 July for most other individuals. The Finance Act, 2026 changed some due dates and time limits for belated and revised returns; confirm them against ICAI material for your attempt.
- **Belated return** attracts a fee (old section 234F: ₹5,000, or ₹1,000 if total income does not exceed ₹5 lakh) and loses carry forward of most losses.
- **Updated return** (old section 139(8A)) lets an assessee add income within the permitted window by paying additional tax.
- Self-assessment tax (section 266 of the 2025 Act; old section 140A) with interest must be paid before filing.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Computing advance tax before deducting TDS.
- Charging 234B when advance tax paid is 90% or more of assessed tax.
- Using the 15 June instalment for a 44AD / 44ADA assessee: they pay 100% by 15 March.
- Charging rebate against special-rate gains under the new regime.
- Forgetting that a fraction of a month counts as a full month for interest.
- Mixing the 12% / 36% tolerance test with the 15% / 45% instalment base under 234C.

keyPoints: Advance tax if liability after TDS >= ₹10,000; 15 / 45 / 75 / 100% by 15 June, 15 Sept, 15 Dec, 15 March.
44AD / 44ADA: 100% advance tax by 15 March.
234A late return, 234B shortfall below 90%, 234C deferment: 1% per month or part.
Return: section 263 of the 2025 Act (old 139); late fee ₹5,000 / ₹1,000.
Order: GTI - deductions = total income; special-rate tax + slab tax - rebate + surcharge + cess - prepaid taxes.

By which date must Ms. Priya pay her advance tax to avoid interest for deferment?
options: 15 June, 15 September, 15 December and 15 March in four instalments
questions.explanation: An assessee under the presumptive scheme for professionals (or small business) pays the whole advance tax by 15 March.

questions.explanation: With cash receipts above 5%, the limit falls to ₹50,00,000. Receipts of ₹60,00,000 would exceed it.

questions.prompt: Mr. Joshi's tax liability for tax year 2026-27 is ₹2,00,000 and TDS on his salary is ₹40,000. What cumulative advance tax should he have paid by 15 September 2026?
questions.explanation: Advance tax payable = 2,00,000 - 40,000 = 1,60,000. Cumulative 45% by 15 September = ₹72,000.

questions.prompt: Mr. Kumar's assessed tax (net of TDS) is ₹1,60,000. He paid advance tax of ₹1,00,000 and paid the balance with his return on 31 July 2027. Compute interest under section 234B of the 1961 Act.
questions.explanation: 90% of assessed tax = 1,44,000; advance tax paid is lower. Shortfall = 60,000. Period April to July 2027 = 4 months. Interest = 60,000 x 1% x 4 = ₹2,400.

questions.prompt: A company pays professional fees of ₹5,00,000 to a resident chartered accountant who has not furnished a PAN. Compute the TDS.
questions.explanation: The normal rate for professional fees is 10%, but without PAN the rate is the higher of 20% and the normal rate: 5,00,000 x 20% = ₹1,00,000.

A resident aged 40 with salary income and tax liability of ₹50,000 after TDS
A firm with tax liability of ₹1,00,000
A non-resident with tax liability of ₹20,000 after TDS
questions.explanation: A resident senior citizen without business or profession income is not liable to pay advance tax.

questions.prompt: TDS on a payment of ₹2,00,000 to an individual contractor for a work contract is:
questions.explanation: Payment to a contractor who is an individual or HUF: 1% = ₹2,000 (old section 194C).

questions.prompt: Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, TDS on salary is governed by:
questions.explanation: Section 392 covers TDS on salary; section 393 covers other payments in a table; section 394 covers TCS; section 263 covers returns.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are consequences of filing a return after the due date? Select all that apply.
options: Interest on unpaid tax for the period of delay
Business loss of that year cannot be carried forward
House property loss of that year cannot be carried forward
The return is treated as invalid
questions.explanation: Late fee and interest under old sections 234F and 234A apply, and most losses (but not house property loss or unabsorbed depreciation) cannot be carried forward. A belated return is still valid.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: advance tax is payable when the tax liability for the year, after TDS and TCS, is ₹___ or more.
questions.explanation: The threshold is ₹10,000.

questions.prompt: Explain the interest payable under sections 234A, 234B and 234C of the 1961 Act.
questions.answer:
- 234A: for filing the return after the due date, simple interest of 1% per month or part on the tax unpaid (after advance tax and TDS), from the day after the due date to the date of filing.
- 234B: if advance tax paid is less than 90% of assessed tax, or none is paid, 1% per month or part on the shortfall from 1 April following the tax year to the date of determination; credit is given for self-assessment tax paid.
- 234C: for deferment of instalments. If cumulative advance tax paid is below 12%, 36%, 75% and 100% by 15 June, 15 September, 15 December and 15 March, interest is 1% per month on the shortfall against 15%, 45%, 75% and 100%, for 3 months each (1 month for the March instalment). Presumptive cases: only the 15 March instalment.
- No 234C interest on shortfall caused by capital gains or winnings arising after an instalment date, if paid in the remaining instalments.
- The 2025 Act retains these interest provisions with new section numbers.
